Robust Uncertainty Quantification for Self-Evolving Large Language Models via Continual Domain Pretraining

Xiaofan Zhou, Lu Cheng Affiliation: University of Illinois at Chicago Correspondence:xzhou77@uic.edu
Abstract

Continual Learning (CL) is essential for enabling self-evolving large language models (LLMs) to adapt and remain effective amid rapid knowledge growth. Yet, despite its importance, little attention has been given to establishing statistical reliability guarantees for LLMs under CL, particularly in the setting of continual domain pretraining (CDP). Conformal Prediction (CP) has shown promise in offering correctness guarantees for LLMs, but it faces major challenges in CDP: testing data often stems from unknown or shifting domain distributions, under which CP may no longer provide valid guarantees. Moreover, when high coverage is required, CP can yield excessively large prediction sets for unanswerable queries, reducing informativeness. To address these challenges, we introduce an adaptive rejection and non-exchangeable CP framework. Our method first estimates the distribution of questions across domains in the test set using transformer-based clustering, then reweights or resamples the calibration data accordingly. Building on this, adaptive rejection CP allows the LLM to selectively abstain from answering when its confidence or competence shifts significantly. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our framework enhances both the effectiveness and reliability of CP under CDP scenarios. Our code is available at: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/CPCL-8C12/

1 Introduction

LLMs have demonstrated impressive performance across diverse domains, from personal assistants Achiam et al. (2023) and robotics Wang et al. (2025) to biology Jung et al. (2024) and scientific discovery Rane et al. (2023). Yet, in the face of rapid knowledge growth, new and private information emerges at a pace that quickly renders their static, pre-trained knowledge outdated. This dynamic landscape underscores the need for self-evolving LLMs that can continuously adapt to novel environments. CL has therefore become a critical capability, allowing LLMs to incorporate new knowledge while preserving previously acquired skills Shi et al. (2024); Gururangan et al. (2021); Li et al. (2023); Lu et al. (2025).

As research on continual learning (CL) for LLMs progresses—particularly in high-stakes domains—the need to robustly quantify uncertainty during the self-evolving process becomes paramount. A central paradigm in uncertainty quantification (UQ) is ensuring that model outputs cover the ground-truth answer with high probability. Conformal Prediction (CP) Zhou et al. (2025); Shafer and Vovk (2008); Angelopoulos and Bates (2021) offers such a framework: a model-agnostic method that provides formal statistical guarantees that the correct answer is included with a user-specified probability. In recent years, CP has been successfully applied across diverse LLM tasks, including multiple-choice QA Kumar et al. (2023); Ye et al. (2024), open-ended QA Su et al. (2024); Li et al. (2024), long-form answering Mohri and Hashimoto (2024); Rubin-Toles et al. (2025), and even LLM-as-a-judge evaluations Sheng et al. (2025), substantially enhancing reliability.

In this work, we study open-ended QA under continual domain pretraining (CDP), a CL setting where LLMs are continually fine-tuned on knowledge from diverse domains. Applying CP to CDP introduces two major challenges: (1) Violation of Exchangeability. CP’s coverage guarantees rely on exchangeability (e.g., I.I.D. data). In CDP, selecting fine-tuning data across domains can break this assumption, leading to uneven coverage across domains (Figure 1). To address this, we propose a non-exchangeable CP framework that leverages a buffer dataset and calibrates using the covariate distribution of the test data. (2) Uninformative Prediction Sets. CP may produce excessively large sets when LLMs face uncertainty in new domains, making predictions uninformative. While adding “Can’t answer” labels can help Li et al. (2024), naive thresholding fails under catastrophic forgetting Toneva et al. (2018). We develop an adaptive CP method based on label-conditional CP Löfström et al. (2015), which dynamically adjusts to shifting model capabilities and achieves optimal efficiency by producing the smallest prediction sets.

Overall, our main contributions are:

  • ∙\bullet

    To the best of our knowledge, this work is the first to investigate CP in the context of CDP for LLMs. We introduce a model-agnostic uncertainty quantification framework tailored to CDP, enabling reliable adaptation of LLMs across evolving domains.

  • ∙\bullet

    We address two key challenges of robust UQ for CDP via CP: non-exchangeability and adaptive rejection under catastrophic forgetting. In addition, we provide a theoretical analysis for guaranteeing better performance of our approach (Appendix A.1).

  • ∙\bullet

    Extensive experiments demonstrate that our approach –AR-NECP–effectively mitigates the distribution shift between calibration and testing data, enabling LLMs to reject unanswerable questions while maintaining reliable correctness coverage.

2 Related work

2.1 CDP in LLM

CDP fine-tunes LLMs sequentially across domains Shi et al. (2024). Gururangan et al. (2020) show that domain-adaptive and task-adaptive pretraining (DAPT, TAPT) consistently enhance downstream performance. To mitigate domain interference, Gururangan et al. (2021) proposes DEMix layers with modular experts that disentangle representations. Qin et al. (2022) present ELLE, which expands model capacity using domain prompts for efficient lifelong adaptation, while recyclable tuning Qin et al. (2023) reuses prior weights via distillation to speed convergence and retain knowledge. Han et al. (2020) introduces ECONET for continual pretraining on temporal and event reasoning. Lu et al. (2025) propose a novel Lora adaptor for dealing with catastrophic forgetting. Domain-specific variants such as PMC-LLaMA Wu et al. (2024), SaulLM-7B Colombo et al. (2024), Lawyer LLaMA Huang et al. (2023), EcomGPT-CT Ma et al. (2023), CFGPT Li et al. (2023), and AF Adapter Yan et al. (2023) further realize vertical continuity, tailoring the pretraining–fine-tuning pipeline to specialized domains while balancing transfer and forgetting.

2.2 CP for LLM

CP enables large language models (LLMs) to produce reliable prediction sets or calibrated outputs Zhou et al. (2025); Campos et al. (2024). Existing CP methods for LLMs fall into three categories: (1) sampling-based CP, which samples multiple responses and selects those exceeding a calibrated uncertainty threshold Su et al. (2024); Li et al. (2024); Gui et al. (2024), though its achievable coverage is limited by model accuracy; (2) adaptive-sampling CP, which continues sampling until reaching the desired coverage Quach et al. (2023) but at high computational cost Su et al. (2024); and (3) abstractive CP, which replaces uncertain content with generic statements in generative tasks Mohri and Hashimoto (2024); Rubin-Toles et al. (2025). Other applications include LLM-as-a judge Sheng et al. (2025), classification, Multi-choice QA Kumar et al. (2023); Ye et al. (2024). However, all these methods assume exchangeability between calibration and test data, which often breaks under domain shifts or CL. As the first CP method for CDP, our method provides approximate finite-sample or global asymptotic coverage guarantees across domains, reduces computation by calibrating once per dataset instead of per instance, and extends CP to LLMs’ CDP—achieving scalable, domain-aware, and more reliable calibration under domain shifts. The most related work is Gao and Liu () that proposes a nearest-neighbor calibration achieving local asymptotic coverage under traditional CL settings.

3 Preliminary

3.1 Background in CP

CP is a model-agnostic framework that provides distribution-free uncertainty quantification with guaranteed coverage Shafer and Vovk (2008); Angelopoulos and Bates (2021). Given a data set {(xi,yi)}i=1n\{(x_{i},y_{i})\}_{i=1}^{n}, it first divides it into training data Dt​r​a​i​n​{(xi,yi)}i=1nt​r​a​i​nD_{train}\{(x_{i},y_{i})\}_{i=1}^{n_{train}}, Dc​a​l​{(xi,yi)}i=1nc​a​lD_{cal}\{(x_{i},y_{i})\}_{i=1}^{n_{cal}} and Dt​e​s​t​{(xi,yi)}i=1nt​e​s​tD_{test}\{(x_{i},y_{i})\}_{i=1}^{n_{test}}, where xix_{i} is the question, yiy_{i} is the corresponding answer to xix_{i}, n∗n_{*} is the number of samples in the corresponding dataset, nn = nt​r​a​i​n+nc​a​l+nt​e​s​tn_{train}+n_{cal}+n_{test}.

Let S⁡(f,(x,y))S(f,(x,y)) denote a nonconformity score that measures how unusual label yy is for input xx under model ff. For example, in classification, it is usually calculated by:

S⁡(f,(x,y))=1−fy​(x),\displaystyle S(f,(x,y))=1-f_{y}(x), (1)

where fy​(x)f_{y}(x) is probability of ff predict xx as yy.

Using the calibration set {(xi,yi)}i=1nc​a​l\{(x_{i},y_{i})\}_{i=1}^{n_{cal}}, it compute non-conformity scores as:

si=S(f,(xi,yi)),i=1,…,nc​a​l.\displaystyle s_{i}=S(f,(x_{i},y_{i})),\quad i=1,\dots,n_{cal}. (2)

Based on the above equation, it calculates a threshold quantile for including labels by:

qα=Q​u​a​n​t​i​l​e​({si}i=1nc​a​l,(nc​a​l+1)​(1−α)nc​a​l).\displaystyle q_{\alpha}=Quantile\!\left(\{s_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n_{cal}};\,\frac{(n_{cal}+1)(1-\alpha)}{n_{cal}}\right). (3)

For a new test input xn+1x_{n+1} and candidate labels y∈Yy\in Y, we compute the non-conformity score for yy as sn+1​(y)=S⁡(f,(xn+1,y))s_{n+1}(y)=S(f,(x_{n+1},y)). Then the prediction set is defined as:

Cα​(xn+1)={y:sn+1​(y)<qα},\displaystyle C_{\alpha}(x_{n+1})=\{y:s_{n+1}(y)<q_{\alpha}\}, (4)

which guarantees finite-sample coverage:

ℙ⁡(yn+1∈Cα​(xn+1))≥1−α.\displaystyle\mathbb{P}\big(y_{n+1}\in C_{\alpha}(x_{n+1})\big)\geq 1-\alpha. (5)

Besides the coverage guarantee, CP also needs to ensure a small prediction set, i.e., high prediction efficiency, to be informative

3.2 Sampling-based CP in LLMs

One common strategy of applying CP in LLMs is to use sampling-based methods, especially for open-ended QA tasks Su et al. (2024); Li et al. (2024). Given an LLM, one would only need two datasets, calibration data Dc​a​l​{(Xi,Yi)}i=1nc​a​lD_{cal}\{(X_{i},Y_{i})\}_{i=1}^{n_{cal}} and Dt​e​s​t​{(Xi,Yi)}i=1nt​e​s​tD_{test}\{(X_{i},Y_{i})\}_{i=1}^{n_{test}}.

It involves two stages, the calibration stage and the testing stage. In the calibration stage, for each data point (Xi,Yi)(X_{i},Y_{i}), it first asks the LLM to generate the answer for MM times, and uses a similarity-based method, e.g., Rouge-L score, cosine similarity, to cluster the answers to get a clustered answer set:

Ci={ci​j|j∈[1,N]},\displaystyle C_{i}=\{c_{ij}|j\in[1,N]\}, (6)

where ci​jc_{i}j is the representative answer in the cluster jj for question ii and NN is the number of clusters. Then it uses the number of answers in each cluster as the uncertainty score, as the clustering may not be perfect, and each question may have various answers. It then calculates the non-conformity score as:

S⁡(f,(x,y))=\displaystyle S(f,(x,y))= (7)
maxj∈[1,M],cj=y⁡(1−freqjM),if such j exists,\displaystyle\max\limits_{j\in[1,M],\,c_{j}=y}\Bigl(1-\tfrac{\text{freq}_{j}}{M}\Bigr),\quad\text{if such $j$ exists},
S⁡(f,(x,y))=0,otherwise.\displaystyle S(f,(x,y))=0,\quad\text{otherwise}.

The quantile is calculated by Eq. 3. In the inference stage, the prediction set is built by:

Cα​(xn+1)={cj:1−freqjM<qα}.\displaystyle C_{\alpha}(x_{n+1})=\{c_{j}:1-\frac{\text{freq}_{j}}{M}<q_{\alpha}\}. (8)

The limitation of this method is that the target coverage is upper-bounded by the model’s ability.

4 Proposed Approach

4.1 Problem Formulation

We consider KK QA datasets Dk,k∈[1,…,K]{D^{k}},k\in[1,...,K], each from different domains, and split them into Dt​r​a​i​nk,Db​u​f​f​e​rk{D^{k}_{train},D^{k}_{buffer}}, where each dataset Dt​r​a​i​nkD^{k}_{train} is used to finetune a corresponding LLM ϕk\phi_{k}, Db​u​f​f​e​rkD^{k}_{buffer} is used to calibrate CP method. At each training step, ϕk\phi_{k} has only limited access to data from previous tasks, which is a common setting in CDP. For illustration simplicity, we describe our proposed CP method on the final finetuned model ϕK\phi_{K}. At this stage, a union dataset DtestD_{\text{test}} containing all domains from previous steps is provided, without domain labels, and an unknown domain distribution. Our goal is to enable LLM ϕK\phi_{K} to generate prediction sets that marginally guarantee to cover the right answer with 1-α\alpha probability.
Exchangeable Assumption within Domains. Our problem setting assumes that data within each domain is exchangeable following Li et al. (2024), i.e., data from calibration and testing sets in the same domain are drawn independently and identically from the same data distribution DD.
Overview. Our framework follows protocols in sampling-based CP and comprises two key components: the Adaptive Rejection CP and the Non-Exchangeable CP modules. The Adaptive Rejection CP introduces a dynamic rejection mechanism that adaptively determines the threshold for abstaining from answering while maintaining the ground truth within the prediction set, thereby ensuring the desired coverage guarantee. The Non-Exchangeable CP component first estimates the domain composition of the testing data by analyzing grouping statistics between the calibration and testing sets. It then either resamples or reweights the calibration samples based on the clustering results from both sets, so that the distribution of nonconformity scores in the calibration data closely aligns with that of the testing data. This adjustment statistically restores exchangeability between the two distributions, enabling reliable coverage under domain shift. The overall procedure of the proposed algorithm is summarized in Algorithm 1. A theoretical analysis of our method for guaranteeing better CP performance can be seen in Appendix A.1.

4.2 Adaptive Rejection CP

A simple abstention baseline assigns a ‘can’t answer’ label using a lightweight MLP’s predicted probability Li et al. (2024), but it lacks a coverage-aware, principled rejection mechanism. We enable refusal via a label-conditional CP scheme calibrated to maintain coverage 1−α1-\alpha on answerable questions; items labeled ‘can’t answer” are then rejected. Concretely, we fix the error rate on answerable instances at (α\alpha)—matching the global CP level—to yield well-calibrated prediction sets. To mitigate catastrophic forgetting across domains, we incorporate the estimated answerability rate from calibration data to adaptively set the rejection threshold. We detail the procedure next.
Rejection Mechanism To begin with, each sample xi∈Dc​a​lx_{i}\in D_{cal} in the dataset is given an unanswerable score sis_{i}. In our project, we propose to use normalized entropy (NE) as the unanswerable score, which is a statistical metric to predict the LLM’s ability to answer a question. It is calculated as:

N​E​(xi)\displaystyle NE(x_{i}) =−1log⁡K∑j=1K|cj|log|cj|,\displaystyle=-\frac{1}{\log K}\sum_{j=1}^{K}|c_{j}|\log|c_{j}|, (9)

where |cj||c_{j}| is the number of answers in cluster cjc_{j}, and KK is the total number of clusters that xix_{i} has. N​E∈[0,1]NE\in[0,1], where higher N​ENE indicates lower confidence to predict the question. We further formulate the probability that the LLM cannot (p0p^{0})/can (p1p^{1}) answer the question as:

p0​(xi)=N​E​(xi);p1​(xi)=1−N​E​(xi).\displaystyle p^{0}(x_{i})=NE(x_{i});p^{1}(x_{i})=1-NE(x_{i}). (10)

Setting the error rate of unanswerable questions as α0\alpha_{0} and the error rate of answerable questions as α1\alpha_{1}, we can get the overall coverage as:

α=(1−rc​o​r​r​e​c​t)​α0+rc​o​r​r​e​c​t​(α1+α−α​α1),\displaystyle\alpha=(1-r_{correct})\alpha_{0}+r_{correct}(\alpha_{1}+\alpha-\alpha\alpha_{1}), (11)

where rc​o​r​r​e​c​tr_{correct} is the ratio of answerable questions in the calibration dataset. Under the exchangeability assumption within domains, Eq. 11 remains valid for the test set. We consider a question as answerable if any sampled question’s answer regex matches the ground truth. Thus, we can get the relation between α0\alpha_{0} and α1\alpha_{1} as:

α1=(1−rc​o​r​r​e​c​t)​(α−α0)rc​o​r​r​e​c​t​(1−α).\displaystyle\alpha_{1}=\frac{(1-r_{correct})(\alpha-\alpha_{0})}{r_{correct}(1-\alpha)}. (12)

After this, we denote the answerable question as x1x^{1} and the unanswerable question as x0x^{0}, with nc​a​l0n^{0}_{cal} as the number of questions that cannot be answered and nc​a​l1n^{1}_{cal} as the number of questions that can be answered in the calibration data. We calculate the quantile for adding the ‘can’t answer’ label as:

qα00=\displaystyle q^{0}_{\alpha_{0}}= (13)
Quantile⁡({p0​(xi0)}i=1nc​a​l0;(nc​a​l0+1)​(1−α0)nc​a​l0),\displaystyle\operatorname{Quantile}\!\left(\{p^{0}(x^{0}_{i})\}_{i=1}^{n^{0}_{cal}};\,\frac{(n^{0}_{cal}+1)(1-\alpha_{0})}{n^{0}_{cal}}\right),

and the quantile for rejecting to answer as:

qα11=\displaystyle q^{1}_{\alpha_{1}}= (14)
Quantile⁡({p1​(xi1)}i=1nc​a​l1;(nc​a​l1+1)​(1−α1)nc​a​l1).\displaystyle\operatorname{Quantile}\!\left(\{p^{1}(x^{1}_{i})\}_{i=1}^{n^{1}_{cal}};\,\frac{(n^{1}_{cal}+1)(1-\alpha_{1})}{n^{1}_{cal}}\right).

In the testing stage, LLM refuses to answer the question when p0​(xi)<qα00p^{0}(x_{i})<q^{0}_{\alpha_{0}} and p1​(xi)>qα11p^{1}(x_{i})>q^{1}_{\alpha_{1}}, where the NE score shows that the LLM has a low probability of answering the question but a high probability of being unanswerable. We add the ‘can’t answer’ label to the prediction set when p0​(xi)<qα00p^{0}(x_{i})<q^{0}_{\alpha_{0}} and p1​(xi)<qα11p^{1}(x_{i})<q^{1}_{\alpha_{1}} to ensure a guaranteed coverage. For the remaining cases, where the LLM has a low probability of being unanswerable, we use the standard CP method.
Prediction Set for Answerable Questions After labeling a portion of questions as unanswerable, some truly answerable questions may be mistakenly classified as unanswerable. This misclassification introduces a distribution bias between the set of all answerable questions and the subset predicted as answerable. To mitigate this bias, we recompute the quantile to ensure that the prediction set properly includes the retained answerable questions, as follows:

q^αt​e​x​t=Quantile⁡({s^i}i=1n^c​a​l;(n^c​a​l+1)​(1−α)n^c​a​l),\displaystyle\hat{q}_{\alpha}^{text}=\operatorname{Quantile}\!\left(\{\hat{s}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{\hat{n}_{cal}};\,\frac{(\hat{n}_{cal}+1)(1-\alpha)}{\hat{n}_{cal}}\right), (15)

where the frequency-based non-conformity score s^i\hat{s}_{i} corresponds to the answerable questions with p1​(xi)<qα11p^{1}(x_{i})<q^{1}_{\alpha_{1}}, and n^c​a​l\hat{n}_{cal} is the number of such questions. For answerable questions, clusters with higher cluster scores than q^αt​e​x​t\hat{q}_{\alpha}^{text} are included in the prediction set cic_{i}, if not rejected. Due to the concentration issue caused by using frequency alone Su et al. (2024), we propose to set the cluster scores as frequency minus NE.
Grid Search for Best Prediction Efficiency With the above quantiles, we use a grid search to achieve the best efficiency (i.e., smallest prediction set), which is especially helpful when the answerable rate is high or the coverage requirement is large, making it hard to find unanswerable questions. Specifically, we choose the pair of (α0,α1)(\alpha_{0},\alpha_{1}) according to Eq. 12. This can be formulated as:

α0,α1=arg⁡minα0,α1⁡E⁡(|Cα​(xi)|∣xi∈Dc​a​l),\displaystyle\alpha_{0},\alpha_{1}=\arg\min_{\alpha_{0},\alpha_{1}}E(|C_{\alpha}(x_{i})|\mid x_{i}\in D_{cal}), (16)

where |Cα​(xi)||C_{\alpha}(x_{i})| is the number of answers in the prediction set for xix_{i}.

4.3 Non-Exchangeable CP Across Domains

In CDP, data from different domains can be non-exchangeable. To achieve reliable coverage across different domains, after each domain’s pretraining, we draw a small subset from DkD^{k} as DbufferkD^{k}_{\text{buffer}}. We further split it into two parts, Dc​l​u​s​t​e​rkD^{k}_{cluster} and DcalkD^{k}_{\text{cal}}, with sizes nc​l​u​s​t​e​rkn^{k}_{cluster} and ncalkn^{k}_{\text{cal}}, respectively. Dc​l​u​s​t​e​rkD^{k}_{cluster} will be used for constructing a cluster centroid for each domain, and DcalkD^{k}_{\text{cal}} will be used to calibrate for CP. Given a joint test question distribution DtestD_{\text{test}}, the domain information is unknown in CDP. Moreover, the exchangeability assumption no longer holds in this setting as testing data and calibration data may have different domain distributions. To address these challenges, we first approximate the domain distribution in the test data and then resample the calibration data accordingly. Our method mitigates the domain distribution shift under the assumption that within each domain, data is exchangeable.
Domain Cluster Centroids via Transformer Encoders. We use a Transformer encoder T⁡(⋅)T(\cdot) to obtain semantic embeddings for all questions, representing each domain in a shared embedding space. For domain kk with nclusterkn_{\text{cluster}}^{k} questions {xik}i=1nclusterk\{x_{i}^{k}\}_{i=1}^{n_{\text{cluster}}^{k}}, each question is encoded as

𝐡ik=T⁡(xik)∈ℝd.\displaystyle\mathbf{h}_{i}^{k}=T(x_{i}^{k})\in\mathbb{R}^{d}. (17)

The domain centroid is then the mean embedding:

𝐜k=1nclusterk​∑i=1nclusterk𝐡ik,\displaystyle\mathbf{c}_{k}=\frac{1}{n_{\text{cluster}}^{k}}\sum_{i=1}^{n_{\text{cluster}}^{k}}\mathbf{h}_{i}^{k}, (18)

which is further ℓ2\ell_{2}-normalized for comparability:

𝐜~k=𝐜k‖𝐜k‖2.\displaystyle\tilde{\mathbf{c}}_{k}=\frac{\mathbf{c}_{k}}{\|\mathbf{c}_{k}\|_{2}}. (19)

A new question xix_{i} is assigned to the domain with the highest cosine similarity:

c⁡(xi)=arg⁡maxk≤K⁡(𝐜~k⊤​𝐡i).\displaystyle c(x_{i})=\arg\max_{k\leq K}(\tilde{\mathbf{c}}_{k}^{\top}\mathbf{h}_{i}). (20)

Testing data domain distribution estimation from the Buffer. After obtaining the cluster centroid for each domain, we group both calibration and testing data according to their nearest domain centroids. Under the I.I.D. assumption within each domain, the statistics of this clustering on the calibration and testing data can be used to estimate the proportion of domains in the testing set.

In the calibration data, after clustering, we obtain each domain’s cluster assignment result. We denote Pi​jP_{ij}, where i,j∈{1,…,K}i,j\in\{1,\dots,K\}, as the ratio of questions from domain ii that are clustered into domain jj. Each domain in the test set will follow a similar transition pattern:

n~testj=∑i=1Kn^testi​Pi​j,\displaystyle\tilde{n}_{\text{test}}^{j}=\sum_{i=1}^{K}\hat{n}_{\text{test}}^{i}P_{ij}, (21)

where n~testj\tilde{n}_{\text{test}}^{j} is the number of test samples clustered into domain jj. Let P=[Pi​j]i,j=1KP=[P_{ij}]_{i,j=1}^{K}, the number of questions in the testing data clustered into domain kk as 𝐧~test=[n~test1,…,n~testK]⊤\tilde{\mathbf{n}}_{\text{test}}=[\tilde{n}_{\text{test}}^{1},\dots,\tilde{n}_{\text{test}}^{K}]^{\top}, and estimate true number of questions in each domain kk in 𝐧^test=[n^test1,…,n^testK]⊤\hat{\mathbf{n}}_{\text{test}}=[\hat{n}_{\text{test}}^{1},\dots,\hat{n}_{\text{test}}^{K}]^{\top}. The system can then be written compactly as:

P⊤​𝐧^test=𝐧~test.\displaystyle P^{\top}\hat{\mathbf{n}}_{\text{test}}=\tilde{\mathbf{n}}_{\text{test}}. (22)

As P⊤P^{\top} is a diagonally dominant matrix, it is invertible Horn and Johnson (2012). We can then estimate the true domain counts by:

𝐧^test=(P⊤)−1​𝐧~test.\displaystyle\hat{\mathbf{n}}_{\text{test}}=(P^{\top})^{-1}\tilde{\mathbf{n}}_{\text{test}}. (23)

Since the transformer-based clustering method demonstrates strong separability performance Wu and Varshney (2024), Eq. 23 holds in practice.
Resampling CP After estimating the number of questions in each domain of the testing data, we resample the calibration data from each domain to form D^calk\hat{D}^{k}_{\text{cal}}. The union D^calunion\hat{D}^{\text{union}}_{\text{cal}} thus approximates the domain distribution of the testing dataset.
Reweighing CP Another approach for alleviating distribution shift in CP is Weighted CP Tibshirani et al. (2019), which reweighs calibration samples based on the estimated domain proportions. Let {si,wi}i=1ncal\{s_{i},w_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n_{\text{cal}}} denote the nonconformity scores and their associated weights, where for each calibration sample xi∈Dcalkx_{i}\in D_{\text{cal}}^{k}, the weight is defined as

wi=n^testk∑k=1Kntestk.\displaystyle w_{i}=\frac{\hat{n}_{\text{test}}^{k}}{\sum_{k=1}^{K}n_{\text{test}}^{k}}. (24)

The weighted quantile threshold q^α\hat{q}_{\alpha} is then

q^α=inf{q∈ℝ:∑i=1ncalwi​𝟏​(si≤q)∑i=1ncalwi≥1−α},\displaystyle\hat{q}_{\alpha}=\inf\left\{q\in\mathbb{R}:\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n_{\text{cal}}}w_{i}\mathbf{1}(s_{i}\leq q)}{\sum_{i=1}^{n_{\text{cal}}}w_{i}}\geq 1-\alpha\right\}, (25)

where 𝟏​(⋅)\mathbf{1}(\cdot) denotes the indicator function. In the Adaptive Rejection CP framework, all thresholds qα00q_{\alpha_{0}}^{0}, qα11q_{\alpha_{1}}^{1}, and q^αtext\hat{q}_{\alpha}^{\text{text}} are recalculated accordingly based on the weighted calibration scores. Compared with resampling-based strategies, Weighted CP provides a deterministic adjustment and generally yields more stable coverage when certain domains in the test set are severely underrepresented, as resampling may fail to include sufficient representative samples from minority domains.

5 Experiment

For a comprehensive evaluation, we focus on the following research questions:

  • ∙\bullet

    RQ. 1. How effective is our AR-NECP method in addressing the distribution shift in CDP?

  • ∙\bullet

    RQ. 2. How does the adaptive rejection CP improve the prediction efficiency of CP (especially on the unanswerable questions)?

  • ∙\bullet

    RQ. 3. How do different UQ methods for LLM answer rejection influence CP’s prediction efficiency?

  • ∙\bullet

    RQ. 4. How well does n^testk\hat{n}^{k}_{\text{test}} (estimated number of test questions per domain) work in practice?

5.1 Experiment Setting

We evaluate AR-NECP on three widely used open QA datasets: TriviaQA Joshi et al. (2017), HotPotQA Yang et al. (2018), and MMLU Hendrycks et al. (2021b); Hendrycks et al. (2021a). For each dataset, we first split it into multiple domains. We divide TriviaQA into five domains using keyword-based search. The corresponding keywords are: science & art (sc), history (ht), sports & politics (sp), entertainment (en), and geography (gg). For HotPotQA, we divide the data into three domains using keyword-based search: science & art (sc), history (ht), entertainment & geography (eg). For MMLU, we follow Liang (2024) and divide the dataset into four domains: STEM (st), Humanities (hu), Social Science (ss), and Other (ot).

For each domain, we set the number of training samples ntraink=10,000n_{\text{train}}^{k}=10{,}000, buffer samples nbufferk=2,000n_{\text{buffer}}^{k}=2{,}000, and both clustering and calibration samples nclusterk=ncalk=1,000n_{\text{cluster}}^{k}=n_{\text{cal}}^{k}=1{,}000, with a unified calibration size ncalunion=5,000n_{\text{cal}}^{\text{union}}=5{,}000. The test size ntestkn_{\text{test}}^{k} will be defined later when we discuss distribution shifts and how our method addresses them. Three LLMs are used: Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3 (Mistral7B) Jiang et al. (2023), gemma-7b-it (gemma7b) Team et al. (2024), and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (Llama8B) Touvron et al. (2023). Our discussion will be focused on results for Llama8B on TriviaQA, and results for the other two models can be found in the Appendix. We fine-tune each model using the hyperparameters provided in the Appendix A.3. We vary error levels α\alpha among [0.05, 0.10, 0.15, 0.20, 0.25].

We compare with two baselines: frequency-based CP (Bad) and basic “can’t answer” CP (Basic), adapting state-of-the-art methods from Su et al. (2024) and Li et al. (2024) to the CDP setting. The former ignores LLMs’ ability to abstain, while the latter introduces a “can’t answer” label but still fails to reject responses when the LLM cannot provide a valid answer. We apply the same data balancing techniques (for addressing non-exchangeability across domains) to all compared methods. Results are averaged from five runs.

Metrics. We adopt three metrics to assess performance: (1) Coverage: the ratio of prediction sets that contain the ground truth. (2) Efficiency: the average size of the prediction sets. (3) Unanswerable efficiency: efficiency measured specifically on unanswerable questions, used to verify the effectiveness of our proposed methods. The first two metrics are standard in CP.

5.2 Main Results (RQ1 & RQ2)

We evaluate coverage and efficiency across different values of α\alpha under three testing distribution settings: (1) When easy questions dominate the test data, calibration causes over-coverage; (2) When hard questions dominate, CP yields under-coverage; and (3) When calibration and test distributions are similar, the target coverage is achieved. For TriviaQA, we set 3000 questions in domain “gg” for the first case and 3000 in “en” for the second, with 200–500 questions randomly sampled for the remaining domains. In the balanced case, each domain contains 800–1500 randomly sampled questions. Results are shown in Figure 2 and Figure 3. We have the following observations:

  • ∙\bullet

    The basic non-balanced CP method is sensitive to distribution shift. When the easier domain (GG) dominates the testing data, it tends to produce over-coverage; whereas when the harder domain (EN) dominates, it fails to reach the target coverage (the dotted line in Figure 2). This confirms that domain distribution indeed affects the coverage and highlights the necessity of addressing such distribution shifts.

  • ∙\bullet

    Both resampling and reweighting methods produce prediction sets whose coverage closely matches the target level, empirically supporting that our approach successfully mitigates non-exchangeability under distribution shift. This also indicates that our estimation of domain proportions performs well in practice.

  • ∙\bullet

    Our adaptive rejection CP consistently yields tighter prediction sets through its rejection mechanism, especially under high coverage requirements, demonstrating the robustness and effectiveness of the grid-search calibration. When the coverage level is low, the improvement becomes limited because the high inclusion threshold already filters out uncertain or unanswerable cases.

  • ∙\bullet

    The Bad CP baseline consistently shows lower efficiency than both the Basic CP and AR-NECP, and fails to achieve the target coverage in most scenarios, revealing the limitations of previous CP settings.

5.3 How do different UQ methods for LLM answer rejection influence prediction efficiency? (RQ3)

We compare two UQ approaches for LLM answer rejection: our proposed method, which uses Normalized Entropy (NE) to measure uncertainty, and a commonly used alternative that trains a small MLP classifier Li et al. (2024) on DclusterunionD_{\text{cluster}}^{\text{union}}—the union of all cluster sets Dclusterk,k∈[1,2,…,K]D_{\text{cluster}}^{k},k\in[1,2,\dots,K]—to predict the LLM’s confidence in answering each question. For illustrative purposes, we evaluated both methods at five different quantile levels using the reweighting strategy. The comparison results, presented in Table 1, show that the NE-based AR-NECP consistently outperforms the MLP-based variant, demonstrating the superior ability of NE to distinguish between answerable and unanswerable questions. The smaller performance gap between AR-NECP (MLP) and AR-NECP (NE) in gg-d domain is mainly because gg is the most recent domain used to finetune LLMs in CDP, making its questions relatively easier for the LLM to answer; hence, the rejection mechanism has a marginal impact.

5.4 How well does n^testk\hat{n}^{k}_{\text{test}} work in practice? (RQ4)

We examine whether estimating the number of test questions per domain is useful in real-world applications. For each testing distribution, we compare the estimated count n^testk\hat{n}^{k}_{\text{test}} with the true count ntestkn^{k}_{\text{test}} in every domain kk and report the mean relative error defined as: Δk=|ntestk−n^testk|ntestk.\Delta^{k}\;=\;\frac{\left|\,n^{k}_{\text{test}}-\hat{n}^{k}_{\text{test}}\,\right|}{n^{k}_{\text{test}}}. Results are presented in Table 2. Overall, the errors are small across domains, which shows the estimator is accurate and useful in practice. The small bias comes from sampling variability; with more samples, for instance, en in en-d, gg in gg-d, the domain-wise I.I.D. assumption holds more closely and the estimates improve.

6 Conclusion

This work takes an important step toward ensuring the reliability of self-evolving LLMs. We are the first to CDP where LLMs must continuously adapt to shifting knowledge domains. Our proposed AR-NECP framework addresses two fundamental barriers: handling unknown domain shifts between calibration and testing data, and enabling LLMs to selectively abstain when their competence varies across domains. By reweighting calibration data according to estimated domain distributions and incorporating a label-conditional rejection mechanism, AR-NECP delivers stronger statistical guarantees and more informative predictions. Extensive experiments verify its robustness and efficiency. Looking forward, this approach opens a pathway toward trustworthy CL, laying the foundation for LLMs that can evolve while maintaining reliability in real-world, dynamically changing environments.

Limitation

There are several limitations in this work that warrant future research. (1) Although our estimated number of test questions per domain is theoretically justified, in practice, it can still exhibit noticeable variance. How to accurately estimate and control this variance is beyond the scope of this paper and can be explored in future work. (2) Another limitation lies in the need to resample calibration answers after each fine-tuning stage on a new dataset, which incurs additional computational cost. Ideally, calibration answers could be sampled once and reused in later stages to improve efficiency. However, this is not feasible because fine-tuning across domains introduces non-exchangeability among models trained at different steps. A potential direction for future research is to estimate and correct this bias by modeling how the number of training steps or the order of domain adaptation affects the calibration consistency.

A.1 Theoretical Proof

In this section, we provide theoretical proofs for the following statements:

  1. 1.

    Our Adaptive Rejection CP can achieve better efficiency than standard CP with the ‘Can’t answer’ label, when the coverage requirement is high and the uncertainty score for identifying unanswerable questions is reasonable.

  2. 2.

    Our Adaptive Rejection CP can achieve the required coverage.

For our Non-exchangeable CP, we additionally prove:

  1. 1.

    Weighted CP achieves global coverage.

  2. 2.

    Resampling CP achieves asymptotic (infinite-sample) coverage.

Coverage Guarantee of Weighted CP.

Under the domain I.I.D. assumption and the explanation in Section 4.3, our estimated n^testk\hat{n}_{\text{test}}^{k} provides a valid approximation of the domain proportions in the testing data Tibshirani et al. (2019). The coverage guarantee of Weighted CP under covariate shift follows directly from prior work Tibshirani et al. (2019). By reweighting calibration samples according to the density ratio between the test and calibration distributions,

w⁡(x)=ptest​(x)pcal​(x),\displaystyle w(x)=\frac{p_{\text{test}}(x)}{p_{\text{cal}}(x)}, (31)

the resulting weighted conformal predictor satisfies the asymptotic coverage guarantee:

ℙ(x,y)∼Ptest​(y∈Cα​(x))≥1−α.\displaystyle\mathbb{P}_{(x,y)\sim P_{\text{test}}}\!\big(y\in C_{\alpha}(x)\big)\geq 1-\alpha. (32)

Coverage Guarantee of Resampled CP.

Under the domain I.I.D. assumption, when the number of resampled calibration samples is sufficiently large, the resampled calibration data approximates the test domain distribution. Hence, calibration and test sets can be regarded as I.I.D., guaranteeing that the prediction set achieves the desired coverage.

A.2 Keywords for dividing datasets into different domains

We categorize the TriviaQA dataset into five domains according to distinctive lexical cues. Science & Art includes a broad range of scientific and artistic terminology, encompassing words such as physics, chemistry, biology, scientist, astronomy, mathematics, theory, planet, galaxy, telescope, microscope, quantum, molecule, enzyme, neuron, genome, DNA, equation, calculus, genetics, and biochemistry, along with artistic and literary terms like poet, poem, novel, novelist, painter, composer, symphony, art, gallery, museum, playwright, theatre, literature, ballet, opera, sonnet, sculpture, poetry, and sculptor. History includes keywords referring to historical eras, figures, and events, including dynasty, emperor, treaty, revolution, war, ancient, medieval, empire, king, queen, monarch, colonial, renaissance, pharaoh, roman, greek, battle, republic, treaties, and monarchy. Sports & Politics merges athletic and political expressions, including olympics, fifa, uefa, nba, mlb, nfl, nhl, footballer, coach, tournament, world cup, premier league, grand slam, stadium, athlete, league, match, finals, medal, goal, club, referee, umpire, arena, president, prime minister, parliament, election, constitution, senate, cabinet, ministry, chancellor, congress, referendum, party, coalition, diplomacy, treaties, regime, governor, and minister. Entertainment focuses on mass media and performing arts, including film, movie, actor, actress, TV, television, oscars, academy award, grammy, emmy, director, screenplay, soundtrack, series, episode, band, album, song, box office, festival, orchestra, opera, musical, and concert. Finally, Geography covers geographic and geopolitical terminology such as capital, river, mount, mountain, province, city, country, island, lake, ocean, sea, peninsula, desert, continent, bay, harbor, border, valley, delta, latitude, longitude, archipelago, and coast.

We categorize the HotpotQA dataset into three semantic domains based on representative keywords. Science & Art contains terms that reflect both scientific and artistic concepts, including physics, chemistry, biology, scientist, astronomy, mathematics, theory, planet, galaxy, telescope, microscope, quantum, enzyme, neuron, genome, DNA, equation, calculus, genetics, biochemistry, poet, poem, painter, composer, symphony, gallery, playwright, ballet, opera, sculpture, poetry, and sculptor.

History focuses on terminology related to historical events, figures, and periods, including dynasty, emperor, treaty, revolution, war, ancient, medieval, empire, king, queen, monarch, colonial, renaissance, pharaoh, roman, greek, battle, republic, treaties, and monarchy. Entertainment & Geography combines cultural and locational entities, covering entertainment-related words such as film, movie, actor, actress, TV, television, oscars, academy award, grammy, emmy, director, screenplay, soundtrack, series, episode, band, album, song, box office, festival, orchestra, opera, musical, concert, and novel, as well as geographical expressions like capital, river, mount, mountain, province, city, country, island, lake, ocean, sea, peninsula, desert, continent, bay, harbor, border, valley, delta, latitude, and longitude.

A.3 Training and sampling detail

The learning rate is set to 1×10−41\times 10^{-4}, and the model is trained for three epochs at each step. During answer sampling, we use a temperature of 1.2, top-p=0.9p=0.9, top-k=100k=100, and a repetition penalty of 1.0.

A.4 Additional experiment on Main (RQ1 & RQ2)

The results of Gemma7B and Mistral7B are shown in Figure 4, 7, 5, 6. They show the same finding as the main text.

The results of Llama8B, Gemma7B, and Mistral7B on HotpotQA are shown in Figures 8, 11, 9, 12, 13, and 10. It is worth noting that HotpotQA is a multi-hop reasoning dataset, which makes it challenging for LLMs to fine-tune effectively. This harder learning problem tends to make the model more resistant to catastrophic forgetting, resulting in minor shifts in the non-conformity score distribution. Therefore, in this dataset, we mainly focus on evaluating the performance of our Adaptive Rejection CP.

In the MMLU dataset, which is a multiple-choice QA benchmark, it is relatively easier for large language models to obtain correct answers through sampling. Therefore, we mainly focus on evaluating our method’s effectiveness in addressing distribution shifts. For efficiency analysis, the coverage results are presented in Figure 14, 16, 18, 15, 17, 19. From these results, we observe that our method effectively mitigates the distribution shift, while also improving efficiency. However, the improvement in efficiency is limited, as the task itself is relatively simple—the model only needs to choose from four possible answers.
